video_title: The technology that could make an international AI slowdown possible
transcript: Tom Reed: Today I’m speaking with Tom Milton, who  is the CEO of Amodo Design, which is a company   that builds hardware for scientific research,  biosecurity, and AI verification. And it is,   above all, the last of these that I’m  interested in talking about with you today,   because I feel like the problem you’re trying to  solve is both very hard and very, very important. Pretty much anytime I look at AI news, it looks  to me like there is another lab CEO, or another   letter signed by thousands of employees, insisting  that they want to slow down the progress of AI   development, but that they are personally unable  to do so for fear of losing the frontier or   ceding the frontier to either another American  company or, really, in the long term, China. And it feels like so much of what we would  want to do on AI safety in basically any   capacity is bottlenecked on this ability to  trust that if everyone wants to slow down,   the other actors are in fact also slowing down. At Amodo, you are building tech which would allow   us to do this. Could you tell me  exactly how this tech might work? Tom Milton: Absolutely. We’ll start by setting  aside the fact that I think a unilateral slowdown   could also be good. We’ll go on from here assuming  that people are shooting for multilateral actions. When we think about a slowdown, the problem  is trust, and therefore the problem is knowing   what is happening at another AI developer, whether  it’s a country or a company. And we can then break   that down into some of the inputs of development.  You could think about the employees as one input;   you think about the software, algorithms, and  data; you could then also think about the compute. And we’re focused on the compute. This is the  physical chips that AI development and deployment   runs on. And this is a really attractive  place to do our verification — to do our   checking whether someone is slowing down — because  they are very specialised to the AI setting. You   need many thousands of them, and at least for  now, they all need to be in the same location.   So it’s a great place to start for monitoring  what different parties are doing on AI. Tom Reed: And so you’re building ways  that you could look at compute and make   claims that would be verifiable  by someone else about what that   compute is being used for. What kinds  of claims would you be aiming to verify? Tom Milton: Exactly. So you’ve said  the word “claims” there. To explain   a bit of language at the top: we say  there is a ‘prover’ who makes a claim,   and a ‘verifier’ who then checks that claim. Tom Reed: Right, so the  prover could be an AI company. Tom Milton: Exactly. It could be an AI  company, whether that’s controlled by a   country or not — essentially the developer. And  then the verifier: this could be another country,   it could be a third party, whether it’s an  embedded auditor or international organisation. And the claims that people want to verify  depend kind of on what your goals are. So   recent examples might be OpenAI claiming that  they have stopped training after their latest   RL [reinforcement learning] accidents.  So you might want to verify the claim,   “We are not doing any reinforcement  learning inside our company.” And as AI safety science advances, I think  we’ll have more specific claims that we want   to verify.So right now we can say this data centre  is on or off: there is no AI activity happening,   or there is some. Or we might want to  go all the way through to details like:   this safety training technique has to happen,  or this type of training technique is too   dangerous and we promise we’re not doing  it. Or these data were held out, or we are   or aren’t using neuralese. But most of that  requires the science of AI development to… Tom Reed: To understand which claims you  would want to be able to make to begin with. Tom Milton: Exactly. Tom Reed: And so the verification R&D  process is allowing us to make more and   more fine-grained claims, so we’re not stuck  at this very costly level of, “The data centre   is literally off, and therefore I know for  sure there’s no training happening there.” Tom Milton: Yeah. When I speak to my non-AI  friends about this, they kind of say,   “Why can’t you just turn it off?” And you  do always have this fallback that you could   turn data centres off. We could turn all  data centres off in the world, but that’s   extremely costly. Inference is valuable,  providing access to the models is valuable. And lots of what verification is doing is  reducing the cost to complying with some kind   of slowdown. So at first it might be turning the  data centre on and off, then it might be serving   only inference — and being able to prove you’re  only serving inference allows you to still serve   inference whilst being worried that training  would be dangerous and should be stopped. Then we might want to do something like resume  small-scale AI safety experiments — alignment   experiments, for example. And this is  where beginning to make more and more   precise claims about how compute is being used  is more and more useful. It both reduces the   cost to coming to a deal, but also opens  up a bunch of value for humanity in still   being able to use the compute for something and  still being able to use the AIs for something. Tom Reed: Great. Let’s zoom in on this example  of trying to verify someone’s claims that they’re   using a given data centre to do inference and not  to do training. And you can imagine this being   useful if OpenAI wanted to verify to someone  that they had in fact paused a training run,   or you could imagine it to be useful in some  grander scenario where the US and China have   agreed to pause training for some amount of time.  AI 2040: Plan A imagines this kind of thing. From what I understand, you’ve built a  prototype that is working towards this,   that could verify that a small cluster of  GPUs is in fact being used for inference   and not training. Could you, at a high  level, walk me through how that would work? Tom Milton: So we’ve got a pilot of a system that  uses what we call “inference recomputation.” If   you were thinking about monitoring the compute,  you could go all the way down to the GPU level,   and you could try and look at the  instructions that are running on the GPU.   We operate at a slightly higher level so that it’s  less invasive, and we look at the network traffic. So there’s this front-end network connecting the  GPUs to each other and also to the outside world.   And we look at the information on that network,  we install a network certifier — what this   basically does is forward on the information to  our verifier node; the information still goes on   to its original destination, it’s just duplicated  — and then on the verifier we run a recomputation. You can think about this as simply rerunning the  inference that happened. So normally your input   tokens go into your model, you do your inference,  and you get your output tokens. What we are doing   is then feeding those through the model again and  checking whether they came out the same. And this   allows us to look at the front-end network,  look at the information on that network,   and confirm whether or not it came from the  model that we all agreed should be running. And of course there’s some nondeterminism in  these models. You need to account for this.   We use an algorithm called DiFR that looks at  some of the probability of choosing different   tokens, and on a long section  of text can have quite high   confidence as to whether these tokens  did indeed come from the right model. Tom Reed: And if no training is happening, then  that model is staying constant, and therefore   you know that it’s only doing inference, because  otherwise the model would be changing over time? Tom Milton: Yeah, so the model staying  constant is one thing. The other thing   is there aren’t packets, bits of information  on that network that can’t be explained by   the recomputation. So another way  of describing this is bounding the   unexplained communication. If you can explain  all of the communication that’s happening,   then you can know that all of that comes from the  agreed inference. If there is this unexplained   information on the network, then there is a  workload that you don’t know about happening. Tom Reed: Interesting. OK, yeah. So just to  lay this out again: you’re claiming to me,   “Here’s the set of GPUs that I have, here’s the  model that I’m serving on these GPUs to these   customers. And you’re going to be able to trust  me, because you are going to have a part within   my data centre where you can rerun the model that  I’m claiming I’m using, and it will produce the   same tokens as the ones that are actually being  sent to external users. And in addition to that,   I can also put network taps into your server,  and they will also be able to certify that   there’s no other things going on other than  the inference that I’m also able to recompute.” Is that correct as a summary?  Have I missed anything? Tom Milton: Yeah, so you’re  coming in to check me — Tom Reed: Let’s say I’m the verifier, yeah. Tom Milton: You’re going to put in your server  that does the rerunning. The network tap — “tap”   stands for “test access point” — is a piece  of fairly standard data centre networking   equipment. And all that’s going to do is forward  the packets on to the verifier. So this is the   piece of equipment that basically bridges your  verifier hardware to my prover hardware. And   the main thing that you’re going to do when  you come in is install that tap to forward   the packets on to you, so you get a copy of them  as well as me having my original copy of them. Tom Reed: And you’ve built a small-scale version  of this and it works. So I would be able to run   this, and whatever you’re running on your GPU,  I don’t need to look into your GPU in any kind   of invasive level of detail. I can just look  at what my own recomputation is providing,   and I can be certain that you’re  running the model that you’re claiming. Tom Milton: Yes, exactly. Tom Reed: What scale does this work at? Tom Milton: So we’ve got this  running on about 30, 32 H100s,   H200s at our demo research cluster in Sheffield. Tom Reed: Great. OK, that’s cool. And are  you hoping that this basic prototype would   be the kind of thing that could be used in  a deal between the US and China? I mean,   this strikes me as requiring quite a lot  of mutual trust. I need to trust that   when I’m putting my server within your data  centre, you’re not then tampering with it.   You need to trust that the network taps  that I’m putting in your data centre,   they’re not somehow picking up on IP  that you don’t want to give to me. Am I right in thinking this  requires a lot of mutual trust? Tom Milton: So I think the things that get  implemented in future deals are likely to,   rather than relying on recomputation,  end up relying on zero-knowledge proofs. Tom Reed: Where recomputation is the  part where I rerun the model weights. Tom Milton: Exactly. And the important part  of this is that rerunning meant that I had   to have access to the model weights  as the verifier. You’re the verifier;   you had to have access to my model. And  it was within the security boundary;   it was within my data centre, so I had some  confidence over the security of the model. I   was fairly sure that by putting it within  my walls, you weren’t stealing the model. But we would much prefer if I  didn’t have to share the model   with you at all. And the way we can do  this is with zero-knowledge proofs. And   there are a few teams already working on  this. We’re working to implement this. Tom Reed: This is ongoing work. There’s  not an established way to do this? Tom Milton: Well, there are some established  zero-knowledge machine learning approaches.   The main problem with what’s kind of  referred to as ZKML, or zero-knowledge   proofs for inference, is that they’re really slow. Tom Reed: They’re very computationally  demanding. There’s a lot of overhead. Tom Milton: Many orders of magnitude  more computational overhead to   run using the zero-knowledge approach.  Although this is coming down, and seems   like something that actually you could  hill-climb with the AIs quite effectively. The reason I’m hopeful on implementing the type of  system we’re talking about is that we don’t need   to check every single packet on the network. So  although it may be thousands of times slower to   generate this proof, actually only checking one  in 1,000 gives us some reasonable confidence. Tom Reed: There’s a way you can sample some of  the packets that are being sent around without   having to do it with every single one, and you  know that they’re not spoofing you in some way. Tom Milton: Exactly. Yeah, subsampling.  And the fraction you need to sample   is roughly on the game theory  you expect of their cheating,   and how worried they’d be about being caught,  and the probability of getting caught. So right now a few of our team are implementing  some of these zero-knowledge proofs on top of   the prototype I just described, so that  rather than having a recomputation server,   that verification server is running  some of this zero-knowledge system,   and therefore the prover doesn’t  need to share the model weights with   the verifier. And that’s going to be much  more palatable on an international scheme. Tom Reed: Great, great. And as I understand  it, this is just one of the ways you could   verify — you’re looking at a specific type  of information, you’re looking at the network   traffic or whatever, to understand  what a data centre is being used for. But I believe we have here with us a prop in  the studio which tries to establish the same   thing — AKA that inference and not training  is happening — by looking at the power that   is consumed by a data centre. Could you  walk me through exactly how that works? And for our audio listeners, we have a prop here.  You can follow along on video if you want to see   exactly what it looks like, but we’ll do our best  to describe it in the requisite level of detail. Tom Milton: Yeah. In addition to monitoring the  network, there are a bunch of other physical   things we could try and monitor about a data  centre and about compute. One would be how the   memory is being used: doing random challenges to  see what’s in memory and then correlate that to   a workload. We can generate these zero-knowledge  proofs. We could do something like proof of work,   which gives you cryptographic proofs that all  of the GPU’s resources are being consumed. And then another thing we can do is monitor  something like power. So the GPU is drawing   a lot of power. We all know that data centres use  lots of power, but as the power is being used, it   fluctuates: the power consumption of the compute  changes with the operations that it’s doing. So in this box here we have a kind of mock setup  of a simple server tray. We have an Nvidia GPU,   a Blackwell series GPU, and the hardware that’s  part of the verification here is this small   inductive loop. So this is wrapped around the  power supply to the GPU. And then we can see on   our oscilloscope here how the power is fluctuating  over time. So we’ve got time on x, and current on   y. And you can see firstly a forward pass,  and then a backwards pass, and then a break. Tom Reed: So what are we running on  this? What did we run on this GPU? Tom Milton: I think we ran nanoGPT or something  — GPT-2 or something like this. And you can see   actually a bunch of properties just from  the power consumption. You can see all of   these little spikes, the really small ones  — that happen at the start of each layer,   and you can actually tell this is  a 12-layer model from those spikes. You see there’s a lot of information that  leaks out of this. In the field of security,   these are referred to as side channels or  covert communication channels. There are   all sorts of crazy ways that nation-states and  other hackers use these to steal information.   But we can also use these as a way to  monitor the workloads that are happening. Tom Reed: And the idea here is that the  amount of power that a given GPU or even   a whole data centre is drawing when it’s doing  a certain action — like a backwards pass — is   distinguishable enough from a forwards pass that  just by looking at the power, you can be like,   “OK, great, there’s no backwards pass  happening here.” Is that correct? Tom Milton: It’s kind of fingerprinting. Workloads  have fingerprints. They have communication   patterns you see on the networks; they have power  patterns as well. And we might not be able to,   at a whole data centre level, tell  this is definitely a backwards pass,   but there are fluctuations that are  canonical — they’re kind of representative,   or are often a fingerprint  of doing different workloads. And another kind of easy example here is  that if you go and read news reports about   frontier data centres, you’ll read about  all of these grid problems that happen   where there are these really large swings  as you do your synchronous training. So   they all do similar actions at the same  time: they all do a bunch of compute,   and then a bunch of stuff moves across the  network while the compute becomes more idle. And you see these big power swings — so much so  that Meta have published loads of papers on how   to mitigate these power swings. So we might not  be able to tell to the fine detail we have here,   because we’re on a single GPU level, but  there are still fingerprints that we can   use to understand what’s going on, and  add this into a scheme like network taps,   or use it as a preliminary tool in the  early stages of some kind of coordination. Tom Reed: Interesting. OK, so my takeaway  from this is that there do in fact exist ways,   if you know that there’s a data centre  that’s being used for some AI activity,   to know from the outside what is going  on in that data centre without requiring   super invasive access. Ideally you’re  going to have some level of cooperation,   but you probably don’t need to let  someone in and see absolutely everything. Tom Milton: The question with access tends to be:  how easy is it to spoof it, and how specific can   your knowledge about what’s happening be. From  this, I think we’re unlikely to know about the   exact details of how fine-tuning is done, or what  data were held out during training, like we did   or didn’t hold out our dangerous biological data.  But we can, for a start, say the data centre is   on or off. We might be able to then say something  more fine-grained, like, “This is consistent with   an inference workload,” “This is consistent  with synchronous workloads like pretraining.” The precision is therefore one  of the things we trade off by not   being inside the data centre. We also  trade off the adversarial robustness,   where by being further away we  have now more opportunities— Tom Reed: It’s easier for them to cheat. Tom Milton: Yeah. If one of the  pretraining teams from one of the   frontier model companies spent a bunch of time  trying to make training look like inference– Tom Reed: As measured by something like power. Tom Milton: Exactly. Would they be able to do  it? I suspect so. They’ll take some efficiency   hit. Whether that efficiency hit is very  small or very large is still up in the air. Tom Reed: Interesting. I’m presuming there  are some kinds of training that look a lot   like inference anyway. If you’re doing  long-horizon RL, doesn’t that end up   looking fairly similar to inference? Again,  depending on how much level of access you have. Tom Milton: In terms of your  rollout and your generating   of your inference tokens, obviously this is– Tom Reed: This is just inference. Tom Milton: We mitigate this in our network  tap recomputation system because the model   weights aren’t updating, which is an important  part of inference. But in this case, because   we’re further away, we have less resolution;  we can make a much less fine-grained claim. Tom Reed: Cool, cool. That makes sense. My overall  take on this is: it does seem like there is a way,   given a data centre that is doing an activity,  to know things about what’s going on in that   data centre. This is a good thing. This  would enable some level of coordination. I feel like the other half of the puzzle  that we would need to know is that there   aren’t data centres somewhere that  we don’t even know about that are   doing things like training. As far as I  understand, this is not something Amodo   is working on. But should we be optimistic  that these are solvable challenges too? Tom Milton: Yeah, this isn’t something we’re  working on. I have a lot of uncertainty here   and get persuaded either way. You talk to  national security people about these things,   and one day they’ll persuade you this is  totally trivial because they’re so good   at spying, and the other day they’ll  say this is just totally impossible:   “There is no way we could  find a hidden data centre.” A few things that helped me  think about this. Firstly,   we will have all of the normal spying resources  — formally called ‘national technical means’:   we will have countries using satellites and human  intelligence and signals intelligence spying– Tom Reed: They’ll be hacking each other. It’s  clearly easy to hack OpenAI anyway, apparently. Tom Milton: Yeah, I mean, the easiest way for  China to know whether US frontier labs are   racing is for them to have terrible security and  for them to just spy on what’s happening anyway. Short of that, there will be some sets of signs  of cheating on deals, I expect. The larger the   project, I imagine the easier it is to catch  a project. Could China hide a $1,000 project?   Presumably yes, that sounds easy. Could they hide  a million-dollar project? Probably. A billion, a   trillion, 10 trillion project — increasingly crazy  numbers seem increasingly difficult to [hide]. I do think the intelligence community will  be able to do a reasonable amount of this.   And under scrambles and quick races to put  together a deal, a very large amount of our   verification and trust in other countries  will come from the intelligence community. Tom Reed: Just unilateral surveillance, basically. Tom Milton: Yeah, exactly. And I’m sure there  will still be networks. I expect the US will   call on the Five Eyes to contribute to their  spying, but there are some mechanisms there. Interestingly, when you talk to national security  people, even the ones who think, “We’re so good   at finding stuff on satellites; you guys just  don’t know how amazing we are at spying” — even   they think it is valuable for people to be  working on stuff in the open. So OSINT, open   source intelligence: there are new projects using  satellite imagery to detect covert data centres. And one of the reasons that they think  this is valuable is because even though   the intelligence community knows something,  that doesn’t mean they can tell the world   about it. And you see this in the nuclear  setting, in which intelligence communities   sometimes commission open source projects so  that there can be some public information. Tom Reed: They commission them to do things that   they actually already know. They just  don’t want to show that they know it. Tom Milton: They can’t show that they know  it because they don’t want to reveal their   sources or methods, or show their  hand. So it might be important that   some of this happens separate to the IC  [intelligence community] so that there   can be international, multilateral, or  public discourse about this information. Tom Reed: The takeaway being that  even if our espionage is good enough,   it would still be very valuable to  have other means of verifying yourself. Tom Milton: Yeah, and I think this should  encourage people who are interested in working on   that to work on it, even though the intelligence  community might do a reasonable job at it. Tom Reed: OK, interesting. So some of these  technical problems may well be solvable,   and we will have ways of verifying these kinds  of claims through espionage, or maybe if we   cooperate enough to install some of this hardware  on each other’s data centres or things like this. But it still feels like the field is incredibly  small. At Amodo, I think you’ve got 50, 60   employees — only some of them are working on  this anyway. And the scales you’re working at,   they’re very small. This here, there’s  just one GPU, right? I’m pointing at   the prop. And your prototype you  said was also pretty small scale. What needs to happen between now and a moment  where we could actually use some of these   prototypes, use some of these technologies, to  verify a literal deal between the US and China? So there’s a lot that needs to occur, right? Tom Milton: Yeah. So I’ll talk a bit about  some of the work that needs to happen,   and then afterwards I’ll talk about  who could do it and who should do it. The technologies that are being developed at  the moment I think are at a kind of prototype   pilot stage. So a few organisations working on  this — I’ll start a list and then inevitably   forget someone. But Lucid Computing are  working on some of these technologies,   including some similar things to what I’ve shown  here. There is the Singapore AI Safety Hub,   who also have a network certifier system,  as do the Future of Life Institute,   are working on some of these technologies.  And finally, a company called Attestable,   who are working on zero-knowledge  proofs for inference and proof of work. These are all at the prototype pilot  stage. I think within a couple of months,   most of them certainly will be at the  point where they can be red-teamed;   they can be tested. So before you get to a  deal, you want all of the parties to trust it,   understand it, and also for it to actually work.  We don’t do red-teaming just to build trust;   we also do it because we do want it to  work, know if it’s actually going to work. Tom Reed: And by red-teaming you mean you  set it up and then you figure out whether   the prover could actually cheat and find a way to  deceive whatever technique you’re using to verify? Tom Milton: Yeah. So in red-teaming, what we  would do is we would set up a pilot installation,   and then we will get an adversarial team  to come and try and break it. And this   can be from either side: either a prover  who tries to cheat the system and do the   illegal workload whilst making  us think it’s the legal one;   or you might also want to red-team from  the other direction, as the verifier,   and try and steal information you shouldn’t be  able to get — steal the model weights or something   like this. And both sides of those might be  important for actual international installations. And we see historical precedent  for this. In the nuclear setting,   the scientists around the world — not just in  the US and the Soviet Union, but in a bunch   of middle powers — were developing tools to  detect whether nuclear tests had happened. And this was important to underpin deals about  test bans — so the Partial Test Ban Treaty,   for example. And these tools are things like  seismology equipment for detecting tremors   in the earth. Before deals happened,  before the US and the Soviet Union   agreed they trusted that this would work,  they ran a Joint Verification Experiment,   in which Soviet scientists went to the US,  US scientists went to the Soviet Union,   and ran tests on one another’s infrastructure.  And I think we’re going to need the same. Tom Reed: They were running a  test on a literal atomic bomb   being detonated and seeing whether their  tools work in measuring the detonation? Tom Milton: Yeah. There are great photos of  them doing these exchanges and having dinners   together and all sorts. And I think we will need  the same between countries ultimately, ideally   between the US and China. I’d be excited  to see the same between AI companies. The near-term version of this is that  a bunch of the organisations working   on this verification tech will be  running exercises in which they   install verification technology  on pilot example data centres,   and then get red teams from the AI companies and  from governments to come and try and break it. And   support from governments and the AI companies  is going to be needed to ensure that happens. Tom Reed: Pretty valuable here. Tom Milton: Yeah, exactly. And each of them have   different knowledge bases that outside of  their setting we don’t necessarily have. Governments have access to the national security  ecosystem. This is interesting for two reasons.   One, they have cyber capabilities that are  unmatched, and having their input on this   is going to be really valuable. And secondly,  they are already well versed in verification. So if we take the UK as an example, there  are departments that deal with both chemical   verification and nuclear verification  for those respective weapons conventions:   [Defence Science and Technology Laboratory] (Dstl)  doing the chemical part, AWE Blacknest doing the   nuclear part. So we have their national security  capabilities that we want to learn from, and also   their verification experience, which is going to  be really invaluable in verification red-teaming. And then in terms of the labs, they have the  infrastructure knowledge, they have the knowledge   on where the frontier is, what the algorithms  look like, and how you might cheat it possibly. Tom Reed: And what sorts of claims you’d want  to make about what it is that you’re doing. Tom Milton: Yeah, absolutely. And  that is invaluable in red-teaming   and testing these systems and making sure  they actually work. We want this to work.   We’re not here to sell a product. This  is all open source IP. We only develop   it because we want it to work. And this  means that collaborations with governments,   labs, other groups who can tell us it  doesn’t work is completely necessary. Tom Reed: Do you have much insight into how  much the labs are doing on verification? Are   they doing verification R&D right now? And  if so, why are they not doing it? Especially   if you’re Anthropic or OpenAI, many members of  your very most senior staff have said that they   want verification technology to exist. What’s  the state of that? How’s that going right now? Tom Milton: Probably if you’re an  outsider looking at the fraction that   the senior staff and the junior staff describe  verification as part of their theory of victory,   you would expect 10 multihundred-person  teams working on this very important thing.   I suspect in reality we see much less  than that, maybe single digits at best. The outside information is scant.  But on the Anthropic side, we see in   their Frontier Safety Roadmap, they talk about  verifiable inference — developing a prototype   by 30 September 2026 that can prove which  model was running. And on the OpenAI side,   we see occasional job openings  that include verification in   the list of tasks, in the RSI [recursive  self-improvement] security engineer area. So I’m hopeful there are a few people coming  onto this yet, but I’m pretty sure there is   not a significant effort that is proportional  to the amount that people talk about this being   necessary, and to the amount that this  is part of people’s theory of victory. Tom Reed: Yeah, I mean, it feels like it’s  almost in almost everyone’s theory of victory,   right? A lot of people believe that there is  a chance that AI progresses blisteringly fast.   Whether or not this happens is unclear. And if  that is possible, then it seems very difficult to   deal with the situation safely at all unless you  can coordinate. So it feels like this is a crucial   element of most people’s theory of victory. Unless  maybe Dario, in his most hawkish of moods, thinks   maybe just winning is all that you need to do.  But I don’t know if this is even what he believes. Tom Milton: I think the bull case, the strongman  case against verification from the labs would be:   we do need to slow down, but  it’s just going to be in the US;   it’s going to be domestic. And in a  domestic case, you can rely on US law,   you can rely on people with guns coming  in and interviewing, and that you don’t   need sophisticated tools on top of embedded  evaluators, for example. And that perhaps   either they’re not actually taking part  in the race, which would be one argument— Tom Reed: “They” being China? Tom Milton: “They” being China.  Or the Dario case, in which   he describes the need for export controls to  make sure that China are a long way behind,   and to extend the lead such that there can be  a domestic slowdown without being worried about   China. And that would be a case where the  importance of verification tools is lower. I do still think the middle powers will want  this. I was making fidget toys,   all sorts. And then fortunately the  US government export-controlled it,   so my psychosis ended, and I was  able to go back to doing normal work. Tom Reed: Enforced cold turkey. Tom Milton: But you don’t really grok how good  the models are until they suddenly are really   good at something that you’re good at, or you’re  adjacent to being good at. So what we’ve done on   this is held 10 hackathons, with six of the  team at a time for a whole day, in which we   just rerun old projects. We get an intuition  for where they’re good and where they’re bad. And it does lead to a weird atmosphere. The  models are really good in some places and   really bad in others. But it is a strange  experience seeing something that you love   doing and are really skilled at suddenly  be done by a computer. So I’m both excited   about the capabilities that we all have, but  also worried and scared about what the future   looks like for a company and for work. I  think this is underrated by many people. Tom Reed: Interesting. So is your  mainline expectation that there’ll   be companies that are good at adopting  this technology into their workflows,   and they will just dramatically outcompete  the companies that won’t? Is this kind of how   you see things going? Or is that  the wrong way to think about it? Tom Milton: I think that is one direction.  I think there’s already slack in the system.   There’s already a lot of waste in the system.  We already outcompete many of our competitors,   and exist because in many cases we’re able  to accelerate scientists by tenfold. So   what’s another fivefold that is caused by models? Tom Reed: How do you measure a tenfold   acceleration of scientists? This  is actually something you measure? Tom Milton: This is something we do. With ARIA, an  ARIA Creator — what they call their grantees — has   to submit milestones that they’re going to hit.  So this is really great for us, because we then go   and help them on one of their projects, and we can  see whether their milestones were delivered early. In a bunch of cases, we’ve delivered milestones 12  months early on a two- or three-year R&D project,   and in some cases delivered things that they  think would have taken 18 months in the course   of a few weeks. So we’re already delivering  very quickly, but haven’t come to dominate   all of science. And this is because of  markets not being perfectly efficient,   all of these other dynamics. So I do think that  companies might be able to move much more quickly. What this means for how your business  models evolve is then an interesting   question in hardware. So we were  originally set up as a consultancy:   we are paid by other people to do hardware R&D  work for them. Increasingly we’re describing   ourselves as a hardware R&D lab or physical  sciences R&D lab now — not least because   “consultancy” is not cool — but because as  we speed up at doing the engineering work   in the middle, we want to take on more  of the upstream and downstream parts. So when we think about our high-impact  work around AI risk, this means taking   more responsibility for identifying the  projects we should work on, more time doing   cause prioritisation and thinking about the  inputs, and then also more time thinking about   the spinouts and how things get deployed. So we  don’t do engineering work for the sake of doing   engineering work. We do engineering work  because we want to see good in the world,   and we can’t necessarily rely on doing  some engineering work, and then putting   the product on a shelf and publishing a nice  GitHub repo with some open source designs. Tom Reed: You want it to go where it needs to go. Tom Milton: Exactly. So increasingly we will  be owning much more of the output. This doesn’t   necessarily mean for-profit spinouts. It could  be for-profit spinouts, it could be nonprofits,   it could be open sourcing designs, it could be  partnering with others for them to deploy it.   And the move to being much faster at the  middle step will mean we can do more of that,   and also take on more of the pie  — more of this impact pipeline. Tom Reed: Taking it back to personalised  hardware, what piece of personalised   hardware are you most excited to build? Do  you have anything that you daydream about? Tom Milton: This was one that I had  for a long time: the wake-up light.   I had thought about making this for years,  and I had just not had the skill set. I   really couldn’t have done that. And now  I have a physical product that’s my own. I recently made a distance tracker for  cycling. So when I go cycling with my partner,   one of us will inevitably drop the other.  And rather than looking behind and always   seeing whether they’re still on your wheel  or you’ve dropped them, I made a system that   uses an ultra-wideband radio. It sits on your  handlebars and it shows how far behind they are. Tom Reed: What is it looking at? Tom Milton: So it has a radio on each handlebar,  and ultra-wideband radios, for some physics   and electronics that I don’t understand, can  tell distance. So one sits on my handlebars,   one sits on her handlebars, and on a little screen  it shows how far behind she is or how far ahead   she is. And then I can tell, “Oh no, I’m cycling  too fast. I’ve dropped her.” Or vice versa. Tom Reed: And that was designed with Fable? Tom Milton: It was designed with Fable. And  there are all sorts of weird products like   this that I’m excited about. And the existence of  these tools, I think, causes a really significant   return to people who have many ideas, who didn’t  necessarily have the execution skill set for it. Tom Reed: It’s the golden  age of the ideas guy, right? Tom Milton: Yeah, exactly. I feel massively  uplifted, but I mostly feel massively uplifted   because I was an incompetent engineer.  Much of our team didn’t feel very uplifted,   but that’s because they were already  very good. So it’s not that helpful. Tom Reed: I’m interested in how you feel  running an engineering company in the UK   right now. How do you feel about the  UK’s prospects going into this world   where AI can do more and more of all the  productive work that humans are doing? Tom Milton: I think at least for the last five  years, being in the UK has been a significant   advantage to us rather than a disadvantage. And  being in Sheffield, in the north of England,   has also been a weird advantage. And the  main weird advantage is it’s not been noisy. So if we were in London, if  we were in San Francisco,   we would have been dragged into a local minima —  dragged into the current venture capitalist hype   cycle. Whereas as a bootstrapped company  in Sheffield, we’ve been able to build an   engine that does amazing hardware work and is  not distracted by the newest ChatGPT wrapper.   And this means we’ve got an amazing team  of 60 who deliver hardware work I think   as well as any team in the Bay would — and  we’ve been able to work on weird things. If we were a venture-backed San Francisco  startup, it’s unlikely that we would have,   at the start of the year, been able  to start working on AI verification   under the premise that maybe you’d need an  international deal. VCs were not into that. So I think being here has given us access to  underpriced talent: really good engineers who   the rest of the world hasn’t noticed. I also  think that our team have honed lots of skills   that don’t get honed if you live in the Bay —  like honest, good delivery that always works. I think the place where this changes is  if frontier AI becomes really important   to our delivery pipeline and the  UK doesn’t get access anymore. Tom Reed: That’s the  existential threat, essentially. Tom Milton: So we already saw this. I  had my three days of Claude psychosis,   where I was using the AI systems to do all of this  electronics design and mechanical design. And then   it was a Saturday morning, I woke up, I said to  Fable 5, “Keep going.” It returned an error. I   said, “Keep going” again; it returned an error.  I went on Twitter: Fable access had been cut off. And suddenly I had lost a skill  set. I had, the previous day,   been able to do some electronic design, and  then I had reverted and I no longer had this   skill. And imagine building a company  on that. You’re building a company on   having access to this intelligence, and it gets  taken away just like that. That is catastrophic. And my worry would be that as frontier AI becomes  more and more capable, the first thing will be   we’ll have a compute crunch. So the US will have  as many data centres as it can, it will be serving   as many tokens as it can, but there will be way  more demand for tokens than there are tokens   that can be served. At this point, what you start  doing is you start prioritising domestic supply.   So instead of serving Amodo with tokens, you  serve your Boston or San Francisco equivalent   with tokens, because you want to develop your own  economy with the amazing hardware progress that   can be enabled by the AIs. And what this means  is that we begin to lose access to AI systems. Now, what can the UK do about  this? Well, of course there is   already a special relationship; there are  already reasonable ties. This is hopeful.   But I think the risk is that the US  are unwilling to export model weights   outside of the US unless you can make very  strong security claims. So the export of the   weights is a marginal cost — unless they get  stolen, in which case that’s catastrophic. So unless the UK has sovereign compute  that is at a high enough security level,   I’m increasingly worried that we will no  longer have access to these frontier models,   and that this could hold back UK science, UK  R&D, UK companies — lower quality of living,   ultimately, as it gets implemented as  part of the healthcare system, et cetera. Tom Reed: So building ultra-secure compute  in the UK would be an absolute priority. Tom Milton: Yeah, I think the case against  this is whether or not you actually need the   frontier of capabilities. Are our engineers  fantastic? Yes. Are they literally the best   people in the world at electronic design?  It’s like, I don’t know, maybe, but possibly   not. Was it OK that we had person number 10 or  person number 100 or person number 1,000? They   were still amazing at doing it. And likewise, I  think we probably see the same with AIs, where   they saturate at a certain point, and some tasks  just don’t benefit from increased intelligence. Tom Reed: There’s not just an infinite  dose-response curve sloping off. Tom Milton: Exactly. So this is where I can  envisage there being much less of a problem   for companies no longer having access  to the frontier. Some problems, they’re   just Sonnet problems. Some problems are Fable  problems, but not all work is a Fable problem. I think it would still be really bad for  your country not to have access to the   smartest intelligence, because there are  many problems that may well yield to these   very significant intelligences. And you  still probably need some domestic compute   for optionality. Even if there is still  a free international market for compute,   you still have a lot of benefit  to having it on sovereign soil. Tom Reed: So it’s still worth  doing even under these conditions. Tom Milton: And I think you also likely need  a bunch of this high-security compute for   your national security as well, where it seems  likely that AI systems will massively transform   the intelligence community. If you think about  their ability to process vast quantities of data   in the same way that analysts do in GCHQ, you  could see them really being bottlenecked by GPU   access. And I don’t think GCHQ are going  to be passing lots of their classified   information through a random Swedish data  centre that’s serving Astra this week. Tom Reed: Well, was it a PLA [People’s  Liberation Army] official who was querying   Moonshot’s Kimi and it ended up going  to Claude? I can’t remember what it was. Tom Milton: Amazing. Tom Reed: Yeah, I can’t remember exactly.  There was some Chinese government official   doing this. So some people are doing this,  but they shouldn’t be, presumably. Yeah. Tom Milton: So I think on the  secure compute side there is this:   make sure we still have access to frontier  models. There is also this clear necessity   for some parts of government to have access  to this for national interest reasons. Tom Reed: Yeah, that sounds  compelling to me. Well, Tom,   it’s been a real pleasure.  Thank you for coming on. Tom Milton: Thank you very much. Tom Reed: Until next time.

transcript_segments.text: Tom Reed: Today I’m speaking with Tom Milton, who  is the CEO of Amodo Design, which is a company
that builds hardware for scientific research,  biosecurity, and AI verification. And it is,
above all, the last of these that I’m  interested in talking about with you today,
because I feel like the problem you’re trying to  solve is both very hard and very, very important.
Pretty much anytime I look at AI news, it looks  to me like there is another lab CEO, or another
letter signed by thousands of employees, insisting  that they want to slow down the progress of AI
development, but that they are personally unable  to do so for fear of losing the frontier or
ceding the frontier to either another American  company or, really, in the long term, China.
And it feels like so much of what we would  want to do on AI safety in basically any
capacity is bottlenecked on this ability to  trust that if everyone wants to slow down,
the other actors are in fact also slowing down.
At Amodo, you are building tech which would allow
us to do this. Could you tell me  exactly how this tech might work?
Tom Milton: Absolutely. We’ll start by setting  aside the fact that I think a unilateral slowdown
could also be good. We’ll go on from here assuming  that people are shooting for multilateral actions.
When we think about a slowdown, the problem  is trust, and therefore the problem is knowing
what is happening at another AI developer, whether  it’s a country or a company. And we can then break
that down into some of the inputs of development.  You could think about the employees as one input;
you think about the software, algorithms, and  data; you could then also think about the compute.
And we’re focused on the compute. This is the  physical chips that AI development and deployment
runs on. And this is a really attractive  place to do our verification — to do our
checking whether someone is slowing down — because  they are very specialised to the AI setting. You
need many thousands of them, and at least for  now, they all need to be in the same location.
So it’s a great place to start for monitoring  what different parties are doing on AI.
Tom Reed: And so you’re building ways  that you could look at compute and make
claims that would be verifiable  by someone else about what that
compute is being used for. What kinds  of claims would you be aiming to verify?
Tom Milton: Exactly. So you’ve said  the word “claims” there. To explain
a bit of language at the top: we say  there is a ‘prover’ who makes a claim,
and a ‘verifier’ who then checks that claim.
Tom Reed: Right, so the  prover could be an AI company.
Tom Milton: Exactly. It could be an AI  company, whether that’s controlled by a
country or not — essentially the developer. And  then the verifier: this could be another country,
it could be a third party, whether it’s an  embedded auditor or international organisation.
And the claims that people want to verify  depend kind of on what your goals are. So
recent examples might be OpenAI claiming that  they have stopped training after their latest
RL [reinforcement learning] accidents.  So you might want to verify the claim,
“We are not doing any reinforcement  learning inside our company.”
And as AI safety science advances, I think  we’ll have more specific claims that we want
to verify.So right now we can say this data centre  is on or off: there is no AI activity happening,
or there is some. Or we might want to  go all the way through to details like:
this safety training technique has to happen,  or this type of training technique is too
dangerous and we promise we’re not doing  it. Or these data were held out, or we are
or aren’t using neuralese. But most of that  requires the science of AI development to…
Tom Reed: To understand which claims you  would want to be able to make to begin with.
Tom Milton: Exactly.
Tom Reed: And so the verification R&D  process is allowing us to make more and
more fine-grained claims, so we’re not stuck  at this very costly level of, “The data centre
is literally off, and therefore I know for  sure there’s no training happening there.”
Tom Milton: Yeah. When I speak to my non-AI  friends about this, they kind of say,
“Why can’t you just turn it off?” And you  do always have this fallback that you could
turn data centres off. We could turn all  data centres off in the world, but that’s
extremely costly. Inference is valuable,  providing access to the models is valuable.
And lots of what verification is doing is  reducing the cost to complying with some kind
of slowdown. So at first it might be turning the  data centre on and off, then it might be serving
only inference — and being able to prove you’re  only serving inference allows you to still serve
inference whilst being worried that training  would be dangerous and should be stopped.
Then we might want to do something like resume  small-scale AI safety experiments — alignment
experiments, for example. And this is  where beginning to make more and more
precise claims about how compute is being used  is more and more useful. It both reduces the
cost to coming to a deal, but also opens  up a bunch of value for humanity in still
being able to use the compute for something and  still being able to use the AIs for something.
Tom Reed: Great. Let’s zoom in on this example  of trying to verify someone’s claims that they’re
using a given data centre to do inference and not  to do training. And you can imagine this being
useful if OpenAI wanted to verify to someone  that they had in fact paused a training run,
or you could imagine it to be useful in some  grander scenario where the US and China have
agreed to pause training for some amount of time.  AI 2040: Plan A imagines this kind of thing.
From what I understand, you’ve built a  prototype that is working towards this,
that could verify that a small cluster of  GPUs is in fact being used for inference
and not training. Could you, at a high  level, walk me through how that would work?
Tom Milton: So we’ve got a pilot of a system that  uses what we call “inference recomputation.” If
you were thinking about monitoring the compute,  you could go all the way down to the GPU level,
and you could try and look at the  instructions that are running on the GPU.
We operate at a slightly higher level so that it’s  less invasive, and we look at the network traffic.
So there’s this front-end network connecting the  GPUs to each other and also to the outside world.
And we look at the information on that network,  we install a network certifier — what this
basically does is forward on the information to  our verifier node; the information still goes on
to its original destination, it’s just duplicated  — and then on the verifier we run a recomputation.
You can think about this as simply rerunning the  inference that happened. So normally your input
tokens go into your model, you do your inference,  and you get your output tokens. What we are doing
is then feeding those through the model again and  checking whether they came out the same. And this
allows us to look at the front-end network,  look at the information on that network,
and confirm whether or not it came from the  model that we all agreed should be running.
And of course there’s some nondeterminism in  these models. You need to account for this.
We use an algorithm called DiFR that looks at  some of the probability of choosing different
tokens, and on a long section  of text can have quite high
confidence as to whether these tokens  did indeed come from the right model.
Tom Reed: And if no training is happening, then  that model is staying constant, and therefore
you know that it’s only doing inference, because  otherwise the model would be changing over time?
Tom Milton: Yeah, so the model staying  constant is one thing. The other thing
is there aren’t packets, bits of information  on that network that can’t be explained by
the recomputation. So another way  of describing this is bounding the
unexplained communication. If you can explain  all of the communication that’s happening,
then you can know that all of that comes from the  agreed inference. If there is this unexplained
information on the network, then there is a  workload that you don’t know about happening.
Tom Reed: Interesting. OK, yeah. So just to  lay this out again: you’re claiming to me,
“Here’s the set of GPUs that I have, here’s the  model that I’m serving on these GPUs to these
customers. And you’re going to be able to trust  me, because you are going to have a part within
my data centre where you can rerun the model that  I’m claiming I’m using, and it will produce the
same tokens as the ones that are actually being  sent to external users. And in addition to that,
I can also put network taps into your server,  and they will also be able to certify that
there’s no other things going on other than  the inference that I’m also able to recompute.”
Is that correct as a summary?  Have I missed anything?
Tom Milton: Yeah, so you’re  coming in to check me —
Tom Reed: Let’s say I’m the verifier, yeah.
Tom Milton: You’re going to put in your server  that does the rerunning. The network tap — “tap”
stands for “test access point” — is a piece  of fairly standard data centre networking
equipment. And all that’s going to do is forward  the packets on to the verifier. So this is the
piece of equipment that basically bridges your  verifier hardware to my prover hardware. And
the main thing that you’re going to do when  you come in is install that tap to forward
the packets on to you, so you get a copy of them  as well as me having my original copy of them.
Tom Reed: And you’ve built a small-scale version  of this and it works. So I would be able to run
this, and whatever you’re running on your GPU,  I don’t need to look into your GPU in any kind
of invasive level of detail. I can just look  at what my own recomputation is providing,
and I can be certain that you’re  running the model that you’re claiming.
Tom Milton: Yes, exactly.
Tom Reed: What scale does this work at?
Tom Milton: So we’ve got this  running on about 30, 32 H100s,
H200s at our demo research cluster in Sheffield.
Tom Reed: Great. OK, that’s cool. And are  you hoping that this basic prototype would
be the kind of thing that could be used in  a deal between the US and China? I mean,
this strikes me as requiring quite a lot  of mutual trust. I need to trust that
when I’m putting my server within your data  centre, you’re not then tampering with it.
You need to trust that the network taps  that I’m putting in your data centre,
they’re not somehow picking up on IP  that you don’t want to give to me.
Am I right in thinking this  requires a lot of mutual trust?
Tom Milton: So I think the things that get  implemented in future deals are likely to,
rather than relying on recomputation,  end up relying on zero-knowledge proofs.
Tom Reed: Where recomputation is the  part where I rerun the model weights.
Tom Milton: Exactly. And the important part  of this is that rerunning meant that I had
to have access to the model weights  as the verifier. You’re the verifier;
you had to have access to my model. And  it was within the security boundary;
it was within my data centre, so I had some  confidence over the security of the model. I
was fairly sure that by putting it within  my walls, you weren’t stealing the model.
But we would much prefer if I  didn’t have to share the model
with you at all. And the way we can do  this is with zero-knowledge proofs. And
there are a few teams already working on  this. We’re working to implement this.
Tom Reed: This is ongoing work. There’s  not an established way to do this?
Tom Milton: Well, there are some established  zero-knowledge machine learning approaches.
The main problem with what’s kind of  referred to as ZKML, or zero-knowledge
proofs for inference, is that they’re really slow.
Tom Reed: They’re very computationally  demanding. There’s a lot of overhead.
Tom Milton: Many orders of magnitude  more computational overhead to
run using the zero-knowledge approach.  Although this is coming down, and seems
like something that actually you could  hill-climb with the AIs quite effectively.
The reason I’m hopeful on implementing the type of  system we’re talking about is that we don’t need
to check every single packet on the network. So  although it may be thousands of times slower to
generate this proof, actually only checking one  in 1,000 gives us some reasonable confidence.
Tom Reed: There’s a way you can sample some of  the packets that are being sent around without
having to do it with every single one, and you  know that they’re not spoofing you in some way.
Tom Milton: Exactly. Yeah, subsampling.  And the fraction you need to sample
is roughly on the game theory  you expect of their cheating,
and how worried they’d be about being caught,  and the probability of getting caught.
So right now a few of our team are implementing  some of these zero-knowledge proofs on top of
the prototype I just described, so that  rather than having a recomputation server,
that verification server is running  some of this zero-knowledge system,
and therefore the prover doesn’t  need to share the model weights with
the verifier. And that’s going to be much  more palatable on an international scheme.
Tom Reed: Great, great. And as I understand  it, this is just one of the ways you could
verify — you’re looking at a specific type  of information, you’re looking at the network
traffic or whatever, to understand  what a data centre is being used for.
But I believe we have here with us a prop in  the studio which tries to establish the same
thing — AKA that inference and not training  is happening — by looking at the power that
is consumed by a data centre. Could you  walk me through exactly how that works?
And for our audio listeners, we have a prop here.  You can follow along on video if you want to see
exactly what it looks like, but we’ll do our best  to describe it in the requisite level of detail.
Tom Milton: Yeah. In addition to monitoring the  network, there are a bunch of other physical
things we could try and monitor about a data  centre and about compute. One would be how the
memory is being used: doing random challenges to  see what’s in memory and then correlate that to
a workload. We can generate these zero-knowledge  proofs. We could do something like proof of work,
which gives you cryptographic proofs that all  of the GPU’s resources are being consumed.
And then another thing we can do is monitor  something like power. So the GPU is drawing
a lot of power. We all know that data centres use  lots of power, but as the power is being used, it
fluctuates: the power consumption of the compute  changes with the operations that it’s doing.
So in this box here we have a kind of mock setup  of a simple server tray. We have an Nvidia GPU,
a Blackwell series GPU, and the hardware that’s  part of the verification here is this small
inductive loop. So this is wrapped around the  power supply to the GPU. And then we can see on
our oscilloscope here how the power is fluctuating  over time. So we’ve got time on x, and current on
y. And you can see firstly a forward pass,  and then a backwards pass, and then a break.
Tom Reed: So what are we running on  this? What did we run on this GPU?
Tom Milton: I think we ran nanoGPT or something  — GPT-2 or something like this. And you can see
actually a bunch of properties just from  the power consumption. You can see all of
these little spikes, the really small ones  — that happen at the start of each layer,
and you can actually tell this is  a 12-layer model from those spikes.
You see there’s a lot of information that  leaks out of this. In the field of security,
these are referred to as side channels or  covert communication channels. There are
all sorts of crazy ways that nation-states and  other hackers use these to steal information.
But we can also use these as a way to  monitor the workloads that are happening.
Tom Reed: And the idea here is that the  amount of power that a given GPU or even
a whole data centre is drawing when it’s doing  a certain action — like a backwards pass — is
distinguishable enough from a forwards pass that  just by looking at the power, you can be like,
“OK, great, there’s no backwards pass  happening here.” Is that correct?
Tom Milton: It’s kind of fingerprinting. Workloads  have fingerprints. They have communication
patterns you see on the networks; they have power  patterns as well. And we might not be able to,
at a whole data centre level, tell  this is definitely a backwards pass,
but there are fluctuations that are  canonical — they’re kind of representative,
or are often a fingerprint  of doing different workloads.
And another kind of easy example here is  that if you go and read news reports about
frontier data centres, you’ll read about  all of these grid problems that happen
where there are these really large swings  as you do your synchronous training. So
they all do similar actions at the same  time: they all do a bunch of compute,
and then a bunch of stuff moves across the  network while the compute becomes more idle.
And you see these big power swings — so much so  that Meta have published loads of papers on how
to mitigate these power swings. So we might not  be able to tell to the fine detail we have here,
because we’re on a single GPU level, but  there are still fingerprints that we can
use to understand what’s going on, and  add this into a scheme like network taps,
or use it as a preliminary tool in the  early stages of some kind of coordination.
Tom Reed: Interesting. OK, so my takeaway  from this is that there do in fact exist ways,
if you know that there’s a data centre  that’s being used for some AI activity,
to know from the outside what is going  on in that data centre without requiring
super invasive access. Ideally you’re  going to have some level of cooperation,
but you probably don’t need to let  someone in and see absolutely everything.
Tom Milton: The question with access tends to be:  how easy is it to spoof it, and how specific can
your knowledge about what’s happening be. From  this, I think we’re unlikely to know about the
exact details of how fine-tuning is done, or what  data were held out during training, like we did
or didn’t hold out our dangerous biological data.  But we can, for a start, say the data centre is
on or off. We might be able to then say something  more fine-grained, like, “This is consistent with
an inference workload,” “This is consistent  with synchronous workloads like pretraining.”
The precision is therefore one  of the things we trade off by not
being inside the data centre. We also  trade off the adversarial robustness,
where by being further away we  have now more opportunities—
Tom Reed: It’s easier for them to cheat.
Tom Milton: Yeah. If one of the  pretraining teams from one of the
frontier model companies spent a bunch of time  trying to make training look like inference–
Tom Reed: As measured by something like power.
Tom Milton: Exactly. Would they be able to do  it? I suspect so. They’ll take some efficiency

Tom Reed: And that basically involves  figuring out ways to prototype things

Tom Milton: Yeah, know how to use  the models, change your scientific

Tom Milton: I was making this  PCB. I was making fidget toys,

Tom Reed: How do you measure a tenfold

Tom Reed: I’m interested in how you feel  running an engineering company in the UK

Tom Reed: That’s the  existential threat, essentially.
Tom Milton: So we already saw this. I  had my three days of Claude psychosis,

Tom Reed: So building ultra-secure compute  in the UK would be an absolute priority.

Tom Reed: There’s not just an infinite  dose-response curve sloping off.
